awd_titl_txt: Doctoral Dissertation Research: Dynamics of Workforce Development
awd_abstract_narration:
This doctoral dissertation research studies the dynamics of workforce development. In addition to providing scientific training for a graduate student in anthropology, the project will inform understandings of corporate-community relations and contribute to the knowledge base that addresses the economic and societal variations in the workforce experience. 

In order to understand workforce dynamics, the investigators utilize multimodal methods that include audio-visual outputs, semi-structured interviews, and behavioral observations. The research expands the anthropological science of workforce development and makes clear contributions to economic anthropology.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

por.por_cntn:
This doctoral dissertation research examined how workers develop, maintain, and transfer specialized skills across changing labor markets in the global mining industry. As industries expand, decline, and relocate across regions and countries, many experienced workers must adapt to new economic opportunities. Through twelve months of ethnographic fieldwork, including extended periods living alongside workers, their families, and their communities, this project explored how technical expertise, workplace relationships, and life experience shape workforce mobility and long-term career transitions.

The research found that skilled workers carry far more than technical knowledge when they move between jobs. Years of experience in mining enabled workers to adapt quickly to new industrial settings because they had already developed practical problem-solving abilities, safety practices, and ways of working that could be applied across different mining environments. These findings suggest that workforce development extends beyond formal training programs and includes knowledge acquired through years of practical experience.

The project also found that access to desirable employment opportunities depends not only on technical ability but also on long-term professional relationships. Workers frequently relied on trusted recommendations, personal networks, and reputations built over many years to secure positions. These findings highlight the importance of social connections and mentorship in workforce development and demonstrate that informal networks continue to play a significant role in labor mobility alongside formal recruitment systems.

Finally, the research documented the long-term effects of industrial restructuring on workers and their families. As domestic mining industries declined, many experienced workers found that the specialized skills they had developed over decades no longer matched opportunities available in local labor markets. Workers who returned home after earning significantly higher wages abroad often found that domestic employment could not match what they had earned overseas, creating a difficult gap between their expectations and the opportunities available to them and their families. The study demonstrates how economic transitions affect not only employment but also workers’ long-term career prospects, family livelihoods, and community well-being.

Beyond its scholarly contributions, the project created a substantial archive of interviews, field notes, photographs, and audiovisual documentation that preserves the experiences of workers undergoing major economic change. More than fifty hours of collaborative video footage were produced with research participants and are being developed into a documentary film that will make the research accessible to audiences beyond academia. This footage was produced in collaboration with research participants who made decisions about what to document and how to represent their own experiences, ensuring that the resulting materials reflect workers’ own perspectives on their lives and labor. The project also generated dissertation chapters and journal manuscripts that will contribute to future research on workforce development, labor mobility, and economic change.

This research advances scientific understanding of workforce development by showing how workers’ accumulated experience, technical knowledge, and professional relationships shape their ability to adapt to changing industries and labor markets. Rather than viewing workforce development solely as formal education or job training, the findings demonstrate the importance of lifelong occupational learning and the social relationships that support career mobility.

Broader Impacts

·   Informing workforce policy: The project provides new evidence on how experienced workers adapt to industrial change, with implications for policymakers designing workforce transition programs for communities affected by industrial decline or economic restructuring.

·   Broadening public understanding of economic change: By focusing on workers’ lived experiences rather than institutions alone, the project offers a human-centered perspective on how global economic transformations affect individuals, families, and communities.

·   Creating publicly accessible research: The project has produced dissertation chapters, journal manuscripts in preparation, and an ethnographic documentary currently in production. These outputs will make the research accessible to both academic and public audiences through publications, educational use, and film screenings.

·   Supporting collaborative research and public engagement: Participants contributed directly to the creation of audiovisual materials documenting their own experiences, helping preserve community histories while expanding public access to research through visual storytelling.
